editorial_rule: An observation is a derived research record, not an original artifact. It must identify the source artifacts it relies on, distinguish independent origins from repeated recitals or copies, and state limits and tests that could weaken or disconfirm it.

items.title: The twelve-year period recurs across the land ownership and possession dispute
items.summary: Twelve years recurs as a legally significant period and as a useful interval to test against the dispute chronology. The recurrence is a pattern for investigation, not a conclusion that every twelve-year interval had the same legal cause or effect.
items.analysis: Separate each proposed interval into its start date, end date, land or parcel concerned, person in possession, asserted legal basis, governing statutory regime, and the event said to start, pause, interrupt or complete the period. Distinguish the statutory rule from dates supplied by judgments, family accounts, registers or later summaries.
items.limits: Repeated references to twelve years do not themselves prove adverse possession, ownership, wrongdoing, or a legally effective interruption. The relevant period and legal rule must be tested claim by claim. Where an earlier order is known only from the 1987 judgment, that is one documentary origin for the recital, not an independently inspected copy of the order.
test_questions: For each proposed twelve-year interval, what is the exact start and end date, and which parcel does it concern?
Which original record supports each date, and is it independent of a later judgment that repeats it?
Which statutory rule applied at the time, and what documented event is said to interrupt or alter the period?
Which intervals fail to reach twelve years, or reach twelve years without the claimed legal consequence?

items.title: Repeated treatment of Mary Williams’s occupation as permissive
items.summary: Several catalogue entries concern the legal characterization of Mary Williams’s occupation as permissive, including accounts of earlier proceedings and later registration. The pattern warrants comparing the wording, date, source and independence of each occurrence.
items.analysis: For each occurrence, record who used the characterization, when, in which document or proceeding, what parcel it referred to, and whether the statement is first-hand evidence, a party's case, a court's finding, a registry entry, or a later repetition. Treat the 1987 judgment and items known only through that judgment as one documentary origin for the recited material. Compare that language with any separately held licence correspondence, title-registration file, possession orders and pleadings before drawing conclusions.
items.limits: This observation does not establish that any person deliberately tried to mischaracterize the occupation. Similar wording may arise from one judgment being repeated in later summaries or records. Motive, dishonesty and legal effect require separate evidence; gaps in the record are not proof of concealment.
test_questions: Which records first use the term “permissive”, and what exact wording do they contain?
Is each occurrence an independent record, or is it a recital copied from EV-0080 or another source?
Does the text concern the same land parcel and time period in each instance?
What original document or contrary record would support or weaken this working observation?

items.title: Name variants and dispersed records complicate the chronology
items.summary: The property and estate appear under multiple names and spellings, while relevant records are spread across different registers, archive catalogues, maps and web themes. That creates a genuine difficulty in linking records and retelling the chronology consistently.
items.analysis: Maintain the exact spelling found in each source, its date, the feature it labels, the archive or register in which it appears, and the reason it has been linked to the Tŷ Mawr / Great House Farm research. Keep uncertain matches visible. The nomenclature index identifies forms including “Cedfin”, “Cydfin”, “Ty Mawr Farm”, “Ty-mawr”, “Great House Farm” and “Cedwyn”; these forms should not automatically be treated as interchangeable in every historical context.
items.limits: Name variation and dispersion explain a cataloguing and chronology problem; they do not by themselves demonstrate deliberate concealment. Similar names can refer to distinct places, and a later catalogue description is not a substitute for the original map, register or deed.
test_questions: Which source uses each form, and what date can actually be assigned to it?
Does the original record name the same building, holding, estate, field or parish?
Are two entries independent records, duplicate descriptions, or archive catalogue copies of the same item?
Which proposed links should remain uncertain until a map or original instrument is examined?

items.title: Sequential parcel capture and permission-framing: the Paper Siege working hypothesis
items.summary: A parcel-by-parcel model tests whether separate conveyances, public-body takings, possession proceedings, licences, registrations and title consolidation progressively reduced the Williams family’s standing on paper while the family continued to occupy or claim land. The model includes the court outcome, competing explanations, source gaps and a separate fiction-only branch. It does not establish a coordinated scheme or wrongdoing.
items.analysis: The model is maintained in data/title-theory.json and published at /wiki/title-theory/. It treats the c.1841 tithe as evidence that John Williams occupied 36 plots, not that he owned all 36. It distinguishes the 1939 fields letting (provisional Parcel B) from the farmhouse/garden claim (provisional Parcel A), and keeps the green as provisional Parcel C. It tests the disputed 1939 signature without presuming forgery; the 1958 Welsh Crichel Down complaint as a reported family allegation; the 1974 licence letters and 1975 conveyance; the 1982–83 first-registration process and notice; the 1987 amalgamation; and the later planning and archaeology chronology. Each causal link has a competing explanation and a falsifier. Death, suppression and hidden-archaeology scenarios are explicitly segregated as unsupported or fiction-only.
items.limits: The complete 1938, 1939, 1969 and 1975 instruments and plans are not all independently inspected; the original 1939 signature and provenance are not authenticated; the full WA231076 and WA240304 registration files and proof of service remain material; the 1955/1962 orders and execution returns need primary inspection; and the reported Neath fire and family-paper loss have not been linked to a common cause. The 1987 Court of Appeal outcome remains the operative legal result. Temporal proximity of deaths to registration or planning is not evidence of homicide.
test_questions: Do the 1938, 1969 and 1975 deeds and plans include the exact same farmhouse, garden, woodland and field parcels later claimed or registered?
Does the original 1939 agreement concern only Parcel B, and is its signature authentic, complete and unaltered?
Who was identified as occupier and claimant in the WA231076 and WA240304 applications, and what notices were served, on whom and when?
Are the alleged permission episodes independent records, or later recitals of the same court judgment?
What contemporaneous records support or contradict the 1958 complaint of wrongful appropriation?
What primary civil, probate, coronial or police records establish the family members’ dates and causes of death?
What do the full archaeological and Neath fire records establish, and is there any documented link to the title dispute?
